segments.text: Friday afternoon, Morgan runs a small community learning program. For this course, we'll follow
Harbor Learning Circle, an illustrative case built from fictional records. Someone suggests adding a
free digital skills session next month. Next three notes are on the table, an attendance count,
a facilitator availability note, and a room capacity note. An assistant can turn those into
to a neat recommendation in seconds.
But if Morgan asks, where did this come from?
A polished paragraph is thin protection.
The work needs a trail.
Our job today is small.
Design one preparation role and one receipt.
The agent does not decide whether the session happens.
It prepares a session option brief for Morgan to review.
That distinction matters.
If we give the system a loose command
like run the workshop program, we have no useful boundary.
What exactly begins its work?
What can it read?
What must it hand back?
Who owns the outcome?
These are ordinary management questions.
They become more urgent when a tool can produce work while nobody is watching.
Write the job in one sentence. When Morgan requests a monthly session review,
prepare one brief comparing a proposed free session
against the three cleared inputs.
The trigger is Morgan's request.
The output is a draft brief.
The manager is Morgan.
The measure is whether Morgan can check the claim
and source for every recommendation
without chasing the agent through a log.
The forbidden actions are just as plain.
No booking, no announcement,
no message to participants,
no spending. A useful agent job names the work it finishes and the work it leaves
alone. Now attach the receipt. Imagine the brief says the room can hold 20 people.
Morgan needs to see which note supplied that number, when the brief was prepared,
what the agent actually did, and whether anyone approved it. The receipt also
records cost or resource use, outcome, and how to pull the draft back. A blank field
stays blank and gets an owner. We never fill a gap with a confident guess. The
first receipt is a handoff a busy person can understand. The engineering log can
remain behind it. In our case, approval is pending Morgan. The outcome is draft
After prepared, no session selected.
The rollback is withdraw the draft from the review folder and mark it superseded.
If the source for room capacity is missing, mark the brief blocked.
A complete-looking card without a source can move bad information faster than an obviously
unfinished one.
The receipt makes that gap visible before anyone treats the draft as a decision.
Take a moment.
Picture one workflow in your own work.
Keep this exercise on paper or in a local draft.
Use a fictional or approved example.
Do not use private operational data.
What is the one useful output and who would have to defend it?
Fill the job and receipt boxes.
Name the trigger, permitted inputs, output, human manager, success check,
and three forbidden actions, then fill the nine receipt fields for one
imaginary run. If you cannot name a source, approval state, or rollback, write
unknown and the person who must resolve it. Do not open a real system to complete
this exercise. The point is to see the shape of the work before asking a tool
to do it. Save those two boxes in your identified operating file as a draft.
Your stop condition is simple. If the owner, source, or review gate is missing,
the draft stays on paper. Next we will name the decision Morgan actually owns.
